item.title: Cunk on Budapest
item.description:
Follow along as I walk around the city of Budapest, a city so wondrous that it makes you wonder: what even is Budap? Is there a city more Budap than this? Or is this really the Budapest of all cities as the name makes it seem?

Budapest is sliced into two halves by the river, The Danube, an exact replica of the river that flows through Vienna: The Danube. This has caused great confusion to river scientists and philosophers alike, because no one knows which is the The Danube. But there is an important difference that they note: unlike the The Danube in Vienna, this The Danube has created two cities. The half of the city I stand on is called Pest, and the half that I’m looking at is called Buda.

Sadly, before they figured out how to call the city by its real name, the ancients who couldn’t be arsed to look at an atlas used to refer to the city as Pest-Buda. That is because they were looking at where I’m standing, standing where I’m looking at. Modern historians now know that was the wrong way to look at it. They also realized after carefully listening to the Hungarians talk that we should be pronouncing the word Pest like “Pesht”. This is a pronunciation tidbit that any tourist who has walked around here for two days seem happy to lecture you about.

Looking across at Pest, standing in Buda, is the gigantic statue of St Gellert, a 11th century Italian bishop. Saint Gellert was a man of God hired by the king to evangelize the pagan peasants of those ancient times. But because it would be many centuries before the Christians would invent the television, the pagans were in-person and responded personally in kind by rolling Mr. Gellert down the hill in a barrel filled with nails. This brings us to another pronunciation tidbit which is that at that moment, St Gellert was pronounced dead.

We are now in Hotel Corinthia Budapest, which inspired the iconic director duo, Wes and her son to direct the movie The “The Grand Budapest Hotel”, a remake of the first ever hotel movie with freaks, The “The Shining”, but abridged for cowards. It is clear to anyone how grand this hotel is, but the puzzle remains: is this Budap enough, and if so, why?

This is the main living room of arguably the grandest and the Budapest complexes of the city of Budapest: The Hungarian parliament. As of 2024, which is the times as I speak, no one is sure who the lead man of this building is, but it is either Viktor or Ban. Since politicians like to hide within the walls of this room, as famine-time emergency supplies, the architects have thoughtfully decked these walls with 40 kilograms of tasty gold. I’n supposed to say “it’s a whopping 40kg of gold”, but I’m not sure 40kg sounds like much. But I’m told otherwise by the little man in my Nokia guide brick they have given us for rent. The little man also says that the building is built with a symmetric design reflecting what was a “bicameral” government until War 2, which means I can just imagine the other half and give my legs a [censored] break. However, since War 2, Hungary has been a “unicameral” government, which is impressive: how do they guard all this gold with one camera?

As you walk away from this building, you will notice two things: your legs hurt like a [censored], and also, installed behind this parliament complex is the mummy of the ex-US president who was involved in the falldown of communism in Hungary. The name: the great insert-adjective Ronald Reagus, named after the economic policies of his time, Reaganomics, which has and will penetrate and widen our societies for years to come.

Note: To be in line with latest legal laws, an instance of the word “[censored]” had to be censored from the last line.

All photos are mine except for the one of that hotel.

item.title: Planets, Dharma and Disaster
item.description:
Every celestial object sails across the sky during the course of a day. But our perceptive ancestors noticed that most do not move relative to each other. It was as if enclosing us earthlings was a mighty, solid, revolving dome—the firmament—and embedded on that ever-turning dome were tiny ever-glowing crystals—the stars—frozen in place.The firmament, a biblical term, finds linguistic kinship in the East: in the Sanskrit word dharma (a complex term that, among many things, means cosmic order, law, duty), and also in the word dharti (the earth). The firmament, dharma and dharti, as their ancient root *dher- suggests, are all a form of support or maintenance, one imaginary, one abstract, and one real.The “fa-dha” kinship parallels the one between the words related to smoke, the Latin fuma and the Sanskrit dhūma.

Our ancestors, staring in wonder at these crystals of light, dreamt of lines connecting them to form shapes, the constellations. These constellations, memorable and recognizable like paintings decorating the inner walls of the dome, reliably guided our ancestors in navigating and ploughing the earth. Reliable they were, because as the dome rotated, so did the stars, but always only as a whole, keeping solid and intact the paintings in our ancestors’ imagination. Some shapes disappeared every dawn overwhelmed by the deluge of sunlight, but they still revealed themselves the next night, solid and intact;These are the circumpolar constellations, like the big dipper, that orient one towards the north or the south. yet others might, one fine night, abandon the sky for months at length, but they still returned a few months later, solid and intact. These are the seasonal constellations, like the constellations along the zodiac belt, whose arrival in a year would mark the beginning or the end of a season.

But our perceptive ancestors noticed on this solid dome a handful of objects that moved relative even to the dome and its orderly stars. These objects, it seemed, possessed a will of their own: they were insubordinate to the rigid shapes, the cosmic order imposed by the human mind onto the heavens. These rebellious travelers of the celestial dome were named after the Greek planan (to wander, to lead astray, to deceive), to become known as the planets,It is imprecise to attribute the “wandering” in this etymology to simply the fact that a planet orbits the sun. It is their relative motion against the celestial map on the dome that gave rise to the idea of “wandering”. their refusal to fit into a constellation most prominent when observing them as they come closest to each other in the sky during what is called a conjunction.This picture of the celestial dome reframes our interpretation of the word disaster (dis + aster). Naively, it conjures the image of an ill-positioned and misaligned star. But in the celestial dome, the stars, which are forced into place on the distant walls of the dome, must themselves bear no fault for their positions; it is the planets, the apparently free-willed entities in the foreground, that must have wandered into an unwelcome constellation to spell disaster.
